name: Yoruba
subtitle: Yoruba: who the sources name, where they live, and what the old labels got wrong.

keyPoints.text: About 40,000,000 people: Estimate of 'the total number of Yoruba people in West Africa' (people, not strictly speakers); no year given in the extract; same page cautions Nigerian census figures are often inaccurate.
Yoruba-speaking communities live mostly in six south-west Nigerian states (Lagos among them), with groups in Benin (formerly Dahomey) and Togo, and a presence in Cuba, Brazil, Haiti and Peru.
The book describes the Yoruba as one of the largest ethnic groups in West Africa with major populations in Nigeria, Benin and Togo.

parts.text: The book describes the Yoruba as one of the largest ethnic groups in West Africa with major populations in Nigeria, Benin and Togo.

Before the 19th century there was no general name for the Yoruba as a whole; the name was first applied to the Oyo (by Fulani or Hausa speakers, per the chapter) and the collective identity dates to the 19th century, shaped by missionaries and the early Yoruba elite.
Origin legend of Oduduwa establishes Ile-Ife as the cradle of the Yoruba; the chapter dates the start of Yoruba history studies to Oduduwa's arrival story and to Crowther and Johnson onwards.
Ife was established around the 11th century and known for its artisans; its heads depict the ooni, rulers of Yoruba kingdoms.

Urbanisation: the chapter describes the Yoruba as highly urbanised, with town unions organised by educated migrants in Lagos and other large towns. (Extract via page summary tool; verify wording before publishing. Ibadan appears only as a dialect area; no readable source on Ibadan/Lagos size.)
Late colonial Yoruba politics cannot be separated from national-level developments and rising ethnic awareness among Nigerians more broadly.
Older city/subgroup identities persisted in dialect and institutions, e.g. Egba (Agbeyin, Gbagura, Oke-Ona) and Ijebu (four provinces) with Osugbo and Ogboni societies in judicial roles.

blocks.q: Myth or fact: That the Ife heads could not have been made by Africans (Frobenius's 1910 theory attributing the Olokun Head to survivors of Atlantis).
blocks.explain: The article calls Frobenius's theories racist and says Ife was known for its artisans and the heads depict ooni, rulers of Yoruba kingdoms.

items.text: Ife established as a kingdom known for its artisans.

Dating given for the Ife bronze (copper-alloy) Ooni head and a terracotta male head; the lost Olokun Head is dated to around 1350 by scholars. (Museum pages from the Met and British Museum were unreadable; this is a magazine caption.)
Major Yoruba polities of the period included Owu, Ijesa, Egba and Ijebu, alongside many smaller polities.
Oyo became a dominant, expansionist polity and, in the 17th century, the main political actor in Yorubaland.
Oyo's collapse was followed by internecine Yoruba wars lasting until British intervention near the century's end.
An inter-colonial boundary divided Western Yoruba into two jurisdictions (today's Nigeria/Benin line, per chapter context).
Lugard consolidated the protectorates into the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria (ceremony in Lagos, 1 Jan 1914).
